statement: Jukurrpa knowledge functioned as accepted legal evidence in the Australian Land Rights (Northern Territory) Act 1976 claims process. The Warlpiri and Kartangarurru-Kurintji Land Claim, lodged 1977 (the second claim heard under the Act), had its report submitted by Aboriginal Land Commissioner Mr Justice John Toohey on 4 August 1978, recommending the grant over mining-company opposition; evidence included named Jukurrpa tracks mapped to specific sites and testimony from named Warlpiri witnesses (Peter Japaljarri, Jimitja Jungarrayi, among others). The related Kaytej Warlpiri Warlmanpa Land Claim (1981) saw women's song series formally tendered as evidence documenting ancestral-being travel and connection to specific sites (e.g. a Rain Dreaming song series to rain-making sites), with ethnomusicologist Dr Richard Moyle testifying on the evidentiary value of song structure and Commissioner Toohey accepting that testimony — a concrete, sourced instance of women's independently held ceremonial/song knowledge functioning as accepted legal evidence. Toohey's reports are credited with articulating the now-standard desert land-tenure model of permanent-water "heartland" sites linked outward by Dreaming tracks of varying length; the kirda (primary owner, patrilineal)/kurdungurlu (manager, matrilineal) system is the operative legal-evidentiary framework, both roles held by men and women according to kinship position, not gender per se.

sources.citation: Aboriginal Land Commissioner (Toohey J.), Warlpiri and Kartangarurru-Kurintji Land Claim report, 4 August 1978, Office of the Aboriginal Land Commissioner (AustLII).
